Learning Objectives
Explain the various treatment options for femoral component revision.
Discuss the indications for different implant types.
Review the clinical outcomes and complications of each implant type.
Introduction

Introduction
Femoral component revision during revision total hip arthroplasty should be performed
via a systematic approach that assesses the amount and location of available bone stock
and considers the options for revision components. A classification system based on the

available host bone may help surgeons develop an algorithm to guide management. In
addition, understanding the options for femoral revision implants is paramount to
developing a systematic framework for successful femoral revision during revision total
hip arthroplasty. (Resources 1 and 2).
The Paprosky classification of femoral bone loss is the preferred method of the authors
of this lesson for categorizing femoral bone loss because it is simple and reproducible
and guides the surgical management of femoral bone loss during femoral revision
(Figure 1). This classification system is based on the amount of available metaphyseal
and diaphyseal bone and requires an understanding of the femoral components
available for revision total hip arthroplasty.
Each revision cementless femoral component has a different geometry and ingrowth
and ongrowth surfaces. The geometry of a stem dictates the location of femoral fixation,
and the surface type dictates the method of biologic fixation. Extensively porous-coated
cylindrical stems achieve diaphyseal fixation via a so-called scratch fit that confers axial
and rotational stability. Splined, tapered stems achieve diaphyseal fixation based on
their tapered geometry, which provides axial stability, and splines, which provide
rotational stability.
Figure 1 Illustrations show the Paprosky classification of femoral bone deficiency. Type I,
minimal loss of metaphyseal bone with an intact diaphysis. Type II, metaphyseal bone
loss with an intact diaphysis. Type IIIA, metaphyseal and diaphyseal bone loss with more
than 4 cm of remaining diaphyseal bone. Type IIIB, metaphyseal and diaphyseal bone
loss with less than 4 cm of remaining diaphyseal bone. Type IV, extensively deficient
metaphyseal and diaphyseal bone. (Reproduced from Keeney JA: Revision total hip

Femoral Reconstruction Options
Cemented Femoral Components
Indications
Low-demand elderly patients
Limited proximal bone loss
Retained cancellous bone
Impaction grafting1
Cementing into an intact cement mantle2
Technique
Remove neocortex formed by prior loose stem, if present.
Preserve remaining cancellous bone.
Use a long-stem prosthesis that extends two to three femoral diameters beyond the prior
stem.3
Use a cement restrictor and current cementation technique to enhance fixation.
Outcomes
Historically poor results with high failure and re-revision rates
Complications
Aseptic loosening: 29% to 39%4,5

Complications
Cemented femoral fixation during revision total hip arthroplasty is reserved for low-
demand patients with minimal proximal femoral bone loss and retained cancellous bone
that can facilitate cement interdigitation. Historical reports suggest high re-revision
rates, with aseptic loosening rates as high as 29% to 39%; however, excellent mid- and
long-term outcomes have been reported if cement is used in patients who undergo
impaction grafting or re-cementing into an intact cement mantle. If cemented fixation is
used in revision arthroplasty, care must be taken to remove the neocortex formed by
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:07 PM
AAOS | Femoral Component Revision
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000507
3/20

the removed stem, if present; preserve remaining cancellous bone; and use a long stem
that extends two to three femoral diameters past the prior stem. A cement restrictor
and modern cementation techniques, such as retrograde filling of the femur and cement
pressurization, should be considered to enhance fixation.
Cylindrical, Extensively Porous-Coated Stems
Indications
Paprosky type I, type II, and type IIIA femoral defects 
Select Paprosky type IIIB femoral defects with canal diameter less than 19 mm6 (Figure 2)
Vancouver type B2 periprosthetic fracture
Technique
Attain diaphyseal fixation distal to proximal bone deficiency
Cylindrical reaming performed to attain distal so-called scratch fit
Requires 4 cm or more to attain reliable fixation
Currently used less frequently because more advanced tapered, fluted modular stems are
easier to use
Outcomes
Excellent long-term outcomes for Paprosky type I, type II, and type IIIA femoral defects: 96%
at 10 years7-9
Poorer long-term outcomes for Paprosky type IIIB and type IV femoral defects6
Complications
Intraoperative fracture: 9%7
Proximal stress shielding
Thigh pain: 16%9

Figure 2 AP radiographs of the left hip of a 59-year-old man with a periprosthetic fracture. A,
Preoperative radiograph demonstrates a periprosthetic fracture with a Paprosky type IIIB femoral
bone defect. B, Postoperative radiograph demonstrates revision surgery with the use of an
extensively porous-coated bowed stem and a cortical strut allograft. C, Radiograph obtained at 5-
year follow-up demonstrates a well-fixed stem with incorporation of the strut allograft.
(Reproduced with permission from Moon KH, Kang JS, Lee SH, Jung SR: Revision total hip
arthroplasty using an extensively porous coated femoral stem. Clin Orthop Surg 2009;1[2]:105-
109.)

Complications
In the past, cylindrical, extensively porous-coated stems have been used broadly to
manage various types of proximal femoral bone loss during revision total hip
arthroplasty. Excellent long-term results have been reported with these stems for
Paprosky type I, type II, type IIIA, and select type IIIB defects (canal diameters less than
19 mm) and Vancouver type B2 periprosthetic femur fractures. These stems allow for
diaphyseal fixation distal to proximal bone deficiency via the use of cylindrical reamers
to prepare the diaphyseal bone to accept the highly porous cylindrical stem and attain a
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:07 PM
AAOS | Femoral Component Revision
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000507
5/20

so-called scratch- fit. Often, 4 cm or more of diaphyseal bone is required to attain
reliable fixation. Despite excellent long-term outcomes, these stems largely have been
replaced by modular and nonmodular tapered fluted stems because of concerns for
intraoperative fracture, proximal stress shielding, and thigh pain associated with
cylindrical designs.
Tapered, fluted Nonmodular Stems
Indications
Paprosky type I, type II, and type IIIA femoral defects (Figure 3)
Select Paprosky type IIIB femoral defects
Technique
Obtain meta-diaphyseal and/or diaphyseal fixation.
Femur preparation using conical reamers to fit tapered stem geometry
Flutes or splines provide implant rotational stability.
Technically more demanding than tapered, fluted modular stems
Outcomes
Excellent long-term outcomes: 92% to 94% stem survival at 10 years10,11
Complications
Stem subsidence
SEND FEEDBACK

Figure 3 AP radiographs of the left hip of a patient with a periprosthetic fracture. A, Preoperative
radiograph demonstrates a loose femoral stem and a Paprosky type IIIA femoral defect. B,
Postoperative radiograph demonstrates revision with the use of a tapered, fluted nonmodular
stem. (Reproduced with permission from Huang Y, Shao H, Zhou Y, Gu J, Tang H, Yang D: Femoral
bone remodeling in revision total hip arthroplasty with use of modular compared with
monoblock tapered fluted titanium stems: The role of stem length and stiffness. J Bone Joint Surg
Am 2019;101[6]:531-538.)

Complications
Tapered, fluted nonmodular stems may be used to manage various femoral bone
defects, including Paprosky type I, type II, type IIIA, and select type IIIB femoral bone loss.
These stems allow for meta-diaphyseal or diaphyseal fixation via the use of conical
reamers that prepare the femur to accept the tapered stem geometry. Longitudinal
splines along the distal tapered portion of the implant provide rotational stability.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:07 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000507
7/20

Excellent long-term outcomes have been reported, with survival rates as high as 92% to
94% at 10-year follow-up.
Tapered, Fluted Modular Stems
Indications
Paprosky type II, type IIIA, and type IIIB femoral defects (Figure 4)
Vancouver type B2 and type B3 periprosthetic fractures
Technique
Obtain meta-diaphyseal and/or diaphyseal fixation.
Femur reamed to accommodate distal tapered segment
Modular junction allows for various proximal body options to attain desired leg length, offset,
and femoral version.
Outcomes
Excellent long-term outcomes: 96% stem survival at 10 years12
Complications
Stem subsidence
Implant fracture: less common with current implants
SEND FEEDBACK

Figure 4 AP radiographs of a right hip with a periprosthetic fracture. A, Preoperative radiograph
demonstrates aseptic loosening of a long, cemented femoral stem with a Paprosky type IIIA
femoral defect. B, Radiograph obtained immediately postoperatively demonstrates a tapered,
fluted modular stem bypassing the zone of compromised bone stock. An extended trochanteric
osteotomy was performed to remove the loose stem. C, Radiograph obtained at 4-year follow-up
demonstrates a well-fixed stem with no evidence of loosening or mechanical complications.
(Reproduced with permission from Otero JE, Martin JR, Rowe TM, Odum SM, Mason JB:
Radiographic and clinical outcomes of modular tapered fluted stems for femoral revision for
Paprosky III and IV femoral defects or Vancouver B2 and B3 femoral fractures. J Arthroplasty
2020;35[4]:1069-1073.)

Complications
Tapered, fluted modular stems are used for various femoral defects, including Paprosky
type II, type IIIA, and type IIIB bone loss. These stems also may be used to manage
Vancouver type B2 and type B3 periprosthetic femur fractures. Similar to nonmodular
tapered stems, these stems allow for meta-diaphyseal or diaphyseal fixation via the use
of conical reamers that prepare the femur to accept the tapered stem geometry. These
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:07 PM
AAOS | Femoral Component Revision
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000507
9/20

stems have a modular proximal segment that allows surgeons to adjust for leg length,
offset, and femoral version through a broad offering of proximal bodies that have
various lengths and diameters. This intraoperative modularity allows surgeons to restore
anatomy, particularly if extensive bone loss is encountered. Excellent survival has been
reported, with large series reporting 96% survival at 10-year follow-up.
Impaction Grafting
Indications
Extensive segmental bone loss 
Contained bone defect
Select uncontained defects that can be converted to a contained defect with the use of mesh
or a cortical strut graft (Figure 5)
Technique
Morselized cancellous bone chips are impacted into the defect (Figure 6).
A tapered femoral stem is cemented into the impacted cancellous neo-medullary canal.
Time consuming and technically challenging
Currently performed less frequently because of successful results with more advanced
tapered, fluted modular stems and proximal femur replacements
Outcomes
Good long-term outcomes: 90% survival at 10 years1
Complications
Periprosthetic fracture
Stem subsidence
Aseptic loosening
Bone resorption
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:07 PM
AAOS | Femoral Component Revision
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000507
10/20

Figure 5 Illustrations show the steps for impaction grafting. A, Morselized cancellous allograft is
impacted into the femur with the use of tamps. B, Sequential broaching is performed to further
impact bone against the endosteal walls, creating a sleeve of bone that can accommodate the
final stem. (Reproduced with permission from Kerboull L, Hamadouche M, and Kerboull M:
Revision arthroplasty with impaction bone grafting and Charnley-Kerboull cemented stem:
Surgical technique and results. Interact Surg 2008;3:72-80.)
Figure 6 Radiographs of a 63-year-old woman with an infected, loose right femoral component.

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000507

A, AP right hip radiograph demonstrates that a stem from ipsilateral total knee arthroplasty
prevented revision with the use of a long, extensively porous-coated implant. A stage 1 revision
was performed with retention of the pedestal to prevent cross-contamination, followed by 6
weeks of intravenous antibiotic agents with subsequent femoral impaction grafting. B, AP right
knee radiograph demonstrate subsequent impaction. C, AP right hip radiographs obtained 3-
months after femoral impaction grafting demonstrates a supplemental strut allograft that was
used to span the stress riser at the distal aspect of the stem. Mesh was used to convert a
proximal medial uncontained calcar defect into a contained defect. (Reproduced with permission
from Scanelli JA, Brown TE: Femoral impaction grafting. World J Orthop 2013;4[1]:7-11.)

Complications
Impaction grafting may be used during femoral revision, particularly if extensive
proximal bone loss is encountered. This technique is not commonly used in the United
States given the technically challenging and time-consuming nature of the technique and
the excellent long-term outcomes associated with simpler techniques, such as modular
and nonmodular tapered fluted stems. The impaction grafting technique involves the
use of morselized cancellous bone chips that are impacted into the femur with tamps,
after which sequential broaching is performed to further impact bone graft into the host
bone to create a sleeve of bone graft that can accommodate the final cemented stem.
This technique allows for reconstitution of femoral bone stock and is associated with
good long-term outcomes, with 90% survival reported at 10-year follow-up; however,
periprosthetic fracture, stem subsidence, aseptic loosening of the femoral component,
and bone resorption are associated with this technique.
Allograft-Prosthetic Composite
Indications
Paprosky type IIIB and type IV femoral deficiency 
Extensive proximal femoral bone loss (Figure 7)
Technique
Long stem is cemented into a proximal femur allograft.
Distal stem is cemented into host bone.
Native trochanter, if present, is fixed to allograft.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:07 PM
AAOS | Femoral Component Revision
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000507
12/20

Currently performed less frequently given the successful results of current proximal femur
replacement
Outcomes
Satisfactory long-term outcomes: 69% to 81%13,14
Complications
Trochanter nonunion: 21%14
Allograft resorption: 13%14
Dislocation: 8%14
Figure 7 Images show the use of an allograft-prosthetic composite to manage proximal femoral
bone loss. A, Preoperative AP radiograph of a left hip demonstrates extensive proximal femur
bone loss. B, Intraoperative photograph shows the allograft-prosthetic composite component
with the trial femoral head. C, Postoperative AP radiograph of the hip demonstrates the allograft-
prosthetic composite cemented into host bone distally with the greater trochanter fixed to the
allograft. (Reproduced with permission from Mayle RE Jr, Paprosky WG. Massive bone loss:
Allograft-prosthetic composites and beyond. J Bone Joint Surg Br 2012;94[11 suppl A]:61-64.)
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:07 PM
AAOS | Femoral Component Revision
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000507
13/20


Complications
Allograft-prosthetic composites may be used if extensive proximal femoral bone loss is
encountered; however, this technique currently is performed less frequently given the
successful outcomes associated with newer proximal femur replacement
megaprosthetic designs. To perform an allograft-prosthetic composite of the proximal
femur, a long stem is cemented into a proximal femur allograft. Next, the distal stem is
cemented into host bone, with care taken to place the allograft in apposition with host
femoral bone stock. If the native trochanter or abductors are present, they are fixed to
the allograft to enhance stability and optimize function; however, this technique is
associated with high complication rates, including trochanteric nonunion, allograft
resorption, and dislocation. Satisfactory long-term outcomes (69% to 81% survival) have
been reported in the literature.
Proximal Femur Replacement
Indications
Paprosky type IIIB and type IV femoral deficiency 
Extensive proximal femoral bone loss (Figure 8)
Vancouver type B3 periprosthetic fracture
Technique
Prosthesis is cemented into remaining host diaphysis.
Abductors or the greater trochanter, if present, are secured to the prosthesis.
Outcomes
Excellent implant survival: 92% at 10 years15
Complications
Dislocation: 14% to 16%15,16
Aseptic loosening: 3% to 8%15,16
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:07 PM
AAOS | Femoral Component Revision
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000507
14/20

Figure 8 AP pelvis radiographs demonstrate modular proximal femur replacement to manage a
loose femoral stem. A, Preoperative radiograph demonstrates extensive left proximal femur
bone loss. B, Postoperative radiograph demonstrates modular left proximal femur replacement.
(Reproduced with permission from Parvizi J, Tarity TD, Slenker N, et al: Proximal femoral
replacement in patients with nonneoplastic conditions. J Bone Joint Surg Am 2007;89[5]:1036-
1043.)

Complications
Proximal femur replacement largely has replaced the allograft-prosthetic composite
technique if extensive proximal femoral bone loss is encountered. This technique is less
technically challenging, reproducible, and associated with a more favorable complication
profile. All damaged nonviable, non-supportive proximal bone is resected, with care
taken to preserve the greater trochanter and abductors if possible. The prosthesis is
placed into the remaining diaphyseal bone, usually with cement, and the greater
trochanter or abductors are fixed to the prosthesis. High rates of dislocation and aseptic
loosening have been reported with this technique; however, excellent long-term survival
(92% at 10-year follow-up) has been reported.
Total Femur Replacement
Indications
Paprosky type IV femoral deficiency

15/20

Interprosthetic femur fracture (Figure 9)
Revision hip arthroplasty with minimal interprosthetic bone stock
Technique
Salvage procedure used for non-supportive femurs or if limited bone stock is encountered
Outcomes
High revision surgery rate: 30% to 50%17,18
Complications
Periprosthetic infection: 33% to 35%17,18
Dislocation: 25%18
Figure 9 Radiographs demonstrate total femur replacement to manage an interprosthetic
femoral fracture. Preoperative AP femur (A) and AP hip (B) radiographs demonstrate an
interprosthetic femur fracture in between a cementless total hip arthroplasty implant and a
cemented distal femur implant. Lateral (C), AP (D), and lateral (E) femur radiographs obtained
after total femur replacement spanning the zone of injury, which was performed resection of the
proximal femur bone stock and femoral stem. (Reproduced with permission from Christ AB,
Mendez L, Gausden EB, Blevins JL, Bostrom MP, Sculco PK: Outcomes and complications following
non-oncologic total femoral replacement. Hip Int 2020;30[6]:725-730.)

Complications
SEND FEEDBACK

16/20

If extensive femoral bone loss is encountered, then total femur replacement may be
indicated, particularly if the femur is non-supportive. This technique involves the use of a
megaprosthetic component that spans the hip joint, entire femur, and knee joint. Given
the invasive nature of this surgical procedure, including large soft-tissue dissection, a
high complication rate has been reported, with periprosthetic joint infection being
reported in 33% to 35% of patients and dislocation being reported in as many as 25% of
patients. In addition, revision rates as high as 30% to 50% have been reported (Resource
3).
